---
title: "Gene Regulation"
description: "How chromatin remodeling complexes find their genomic targets and how their assembly is regulated."
image: featured.jpg
---

The SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex is an enzyme that
slides and evicts nucleosomes to open chromatin for other factors, so that
changes in gene expression follow changes in accessibility. We're interested in finding how this complex  transcription while accessibility stays the
same. The complex therefore also acts as a scaffold, recruiting regulatory
proteins independently of its remodeling activity. We study what controls that
scaffolding and how the partners SWI/SNF recruits produce specific changes in
gene expression.

Our current projects focus on two ways SWI/SNF  partners are regulated.
One is post-translational modification of SWI/SNF subunits. CARM1 methylates an
arginine on the core subunit BAF155. This methylation does not change which
version of the complex assembles, but it changes the proteins the complex
contacts, particularly the RNA processing machinery, and can alter
transcription without any change in chromatin accessibility. The other input is
RNA itself. SWI/SNF and related remodelers bind RNA and act at several steps of the
transcription cycle, including polymerase pausing, splicing, and 3′ end
processing, and RNA can tune the complex's interactions on a
transcript-by-transcript basis.

Our goal is to define how SWI/SNF and related remodelers select their regulatory
partners and how that selection shapes gene regulation beyond accessibility. We
use chromatin profiling, gene expression analysis, and interaction proteomics to
link specific modifications and RNA contacts to the genes they control.
